hero.headline: I-95 South lanes reopen in Delray Beach after crash causes injuries Thursday morning
hero.teaser: Multiple lanes of I-95 South in Delray Beach were blocked due to a crash with injuries Thursday morning just before the Atlantic Avenue exit.
hero.body:
The accident occurred at around 6 a.m. just before the Atlantic Avenue exit on I-95 South in Delray Beach, prompting four lanes to shut down. There were injuries as a result of the crash, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.

As of 6:25 a.m., all lanes are back open. The crash blocked multiple lanes during the Thursday morning commute before crews cleared the scene.

cards.headline: Driver crashes into Hobe Sound water plant, hundreds lose service before arrest
cards.teaser: A Stuart man crashed into a large pipe at the Hobe Sound/Osprey Water Plant at around 9 p.m.
cards.body:
A driver crashed into a large pipe at the Hobe Sound/Osprey Water Plant around 9 p.m. Wednesday and fled the scene, leaving hundreds of homes without water service or adequate water pressure, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The crash caused a break in water service across the area. Eliuvar Garza, 24, of Stuart, has been charged with leaving the scene of a crash with property damage, driving with a suspended license with knowledge, failure to use due care, and failure to stop at a stop sign. A witness reported that the individual repeatedly stated "I messed up" before running from the scene. Garza was located when a family member brought him to the hospital for injuries associated with the crash.

Water services are now fully restored in the area, according to the South Martin Regional Utility (SMRU). SMRU posted an advisory on its website stating that customers affected by the water shortage should boil their water for three minutes before using it. "The SMRU emergency response team has restored water to all customers affected by this incident," the advisory stated. The boil water warning is in effect until further notice. Hobe Sound residents with questions about their water service should contact the water company directly.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound under boil water notice after driver crashes into water plant pipe
cards.body:
A vehicle struck a major pipe at the Hobe Sound/Osprey Water Plant on Wednesday night, causing the driver to abandon the scene and leaving hundreds of residents without water service or adequate water pressure. The Martin County Sheriff's Office responded to the crash, which occurred around 9 p.m.

Investigators located the driver through a hospital visit. The driver, 24-year-old Eliuvar Garza of Stuart, was brought to the hospital by a family member for injuries sustained in the crash. According to witness accounts, Garza repeatedly said "I messed up" before fleeing the scene. He now faces multiple charges including leaving the scene of a crash with property damage, driving with a suspended license with knowledge of the suspension, failure to use due care, and failure to stop at a stop sign.

The South Martin Regional Utility has restored water service to all affected customers in the area. However, the utility issued an advisory for residents who experienced the water shortage. Customers should boil their water for three minutes before using it, according to the advisory posted on the SMRU website. The emergency response team worked to restore water to every household impacted by the pipe damage.

The boil water warning remains in effect until further notice. Any Hobe Sound residents with questions about their water service should contact the South Martin Regional Utility directly for more information.

cards.headline: Miami-Dade plans permanent conservation use for Alligator Alcatraz site after detention center closure
cards.body:
Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava announced plans to transfer all county-owned land at the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport to the National Park Service or other Everglades restoration partners once the Alligator Alcatraz immigration detention facility closes. In a Thursday memo to County Commissioners, Levine Cava stated her administration intends to pursue the transfer of the roughly 17,000-acre wetlands area within Big Cypress National Preserve for permanent conservation use as part of the Central Everglades Restoration Plan.

Levine Cava argued that the remote site has limited value as an aviation asset, pointing to high maintenance costs and flight restrictions due to its location near sensitive wetlands. She wrote that returning the lands to conservation represents "a historic opportunity to permanently protect these lands and contribute meaningfully to one of the most ambitious environmental restoration efforts in the nation." The transfer would also reduce county liabilities associated with managing an aviation facility with minimal strategic utility while creating opportunities to leverage federal restoration funding. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed that all detainees at the facility had been transferred to federal sites for their safety ahead of hurricane season.

The facility opened July 3, 2025, and has faced harsh criticism from lawyers, families and human rights groups over conditions and treatment of detainees. Detainees have reported poor physical conditions including worms in food, nonfunctioning toilets, flooding with fecal waste, and pervasive mosquitoes and insects. The detention center has cost far more than anticipated, with vendor contracts exceeding 824 million dollars for operations and maintenance alone, not including construction. According to an analysis by The Atlantic, the expenses were so high that it would have been cheaper to purchase each of the approximately 1,800 men detained there a one-bedroom condominium in Orlando and pay for a full-time personal guard. Florida has been approved for 608 million dollars in reimbursements but has received only 58.2 million dollars so far.

Levine Cava's administration will work with the County Attorney's Office and state and federal partners to identify legal transfer mechanisms, including conservation easements, deed restrictions, intergovernmental agreements, land exchanges or direct conveyance. Her office will provide formal recommendations to the Commission in the coming months. The transfer would permanently remove the lands from future detention, industrial or intensive commercial development and dedicate them to ecological restoration, habitat preservation and environmental protection.

cards.headline: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League urges South Florida pet owners to prepare hurricane disaster plans
cards.teaser: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create a disaster plan for their pets before the next storm hits. The safest place for pets during a hurricane is right alongside their owners, according to CEO Dr. Alyssa Comroe.
cards.body:
As hurricane season approaches, Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is calling on South Florida residents to develop comprehensive disaster plans for their pets before the next storm arrives. Dr. Alyssa Comroe, the organization's CEO, emphasized to WPTV that pets should remain with their owners throughout a hurricane rather than being left behind or separated during evacuation. The shelter's team of experts has identified several essential steps that pet owners should take now to protect their animals when severe weather strikes.

Proper identification is the foundation of pet safety during hurricanes. The rescue league recommends that all pets wear collars with current identification information and have updated microchips registered with accurate contact details. Additionally, pet owners should familiarize their animals with a designated safe room in advance, such as a walk-in closet or downstairs bathroom. Conducting practice runs before an actual hurricane ensures that pets will be comfortable entering this space when needed and reduces their stress during the actual emergency.

Preparing a dedicated pet emergency kit is equally important. This kit should contain a three-day supply of food and water stored in airtight containers, food and water bowls, a sturdy carrier for transport, bedding, towels, and two weeks' worth of any necessary medications. Pet owners should also include vaccination records, first-aid supplies, and for cat owners, litter and a litter box. The kit should have leashes, harnesses, cool packs, wipes, waste bags, and multiple forms of visible identification. Beyond physical supplies, pet owners should maintain a printed list of local pet-friendly shelters and hotels in an easily accessible location and keep recent photographs of their pets, ideally showing the animal with their owner, to aid in identification if pets become separated.

Storm preparedness should include practicing regular hurricane drills that incorporate pets' daily routines. Running through feeding schedules, water provision, and rest periods inside the safe room helps pets acclimate and maximizes their comfort during an actual emergency. With Florida's hurricane season running from June through November and overlapping with extreme summer heat, pet owners should also implement year-round heat safety measures including water enrichment, adequate shade, and limiting outdoor activity during the hottest parts of the day. Taking these proactive steps now can significantly reduce risks during evacuations and help ensure that pets remain safe and healthy throughout severe weather events.

cards.headline: 67-year-old man killed in eight-vehicle pileup on Dixie Highway in Lantana
cards.teaser: Surveillance video captured a Jeep Wrangler speeding at an estimated 100 mph before triggering a deadly crash that left one man dead and others seriously hurt.
cards.body:
A Jeep Wrangler struck a truck near Ocean Avenue and Dixie Highway in Lantana on Tuesday, triggering an eight-vehicle pileup that killed 67-year-old Jose Bedoya and seriously injured two others. Investigators say the Jeep hit the truck, fled the scene, then slammed into stopped traffic. Sal Perna, who owns a car rental business near the scene, witnessed the Jeep traveling at extreme speeds before the crash. "I saw this Jeep, 4-door Jeep go by here at I would guesstimate 100 mph," Perna said. He described the destruction as unlike anything he had seen in his 11 years at the location, saying vehicles were unrecognizable.

Bedoya's son shared a statement remembering his father as "the most hard working selfless person to ever exist" and "the most patient and humble man to ever roam earth." A GoFundMe has been set up to support his family. Perna is now calling for increased police presence on Dixie Highway, saying dangerous driving is a daily occurrence. "11 years I've been sitting at this desk and every day I see people spending 50, 60, 70 miles an hour," Perna said. "Something needs to be done." Investigators confirmed the case remains an ongoing, active investigation.

cards.headline: Strong storms topple trees and damage property in Royal Palm Beach and Wellington
cards.teaser: Thunderstorms swept through Royal Palm Beach and Wellington Wednesday night, blocking roads with fallen trees and causing widespread damage to fences and light poles.
cards.body:
Strong thunderstorms swept through Royal Palm Beach and Wellington Wednesday night, toppling trees, twisting fences and knocking down light poles across both communities. Hail pelted cars, lightning struck close to residents and strong winds caused widespread damage throughout the area. In one Royal Palm Beach neighborhood, a large tree was uprooted and fell into the road, blocking traffic. Firefighters responded and pulled the tree from the road so neighbors could clear it. The tree fell in front of a car driving down the street in front of the home of seven-year-old Danny Jaworski and his grandmother.

Danny's mother, Leslie Jaworski, owns the home, which had been named the neighborhood's Home of the Month. She was at work when the storm hit and came home to find firefighters already on scene working to clear the tree. "I was grateful that the tree didn't go this way and land on my roof, because I've heard horror stories of that," Leslie said. She added that she was grateful traffic was able to get through. The experience has her thinking ahead to future storms. "I'm a new homeowner, so it does kind of make me worried about future storms and what can happen," Leslie said.

hero.headline: Jupiter Medical Center breaks ground on hospital in western Palm Beach Gardens
hero.teaser: Jupiter Medical Center held a groundbreaking ceremony Wednesday for a new neighborhood hospital in the Avenir community off Northlake Boulevard, expected to serve approximately 40,000 residents.
hero.body:
Jupiter Medical Center held a groundbreaking ceremony Wednesday to launch construction on a new hospital in western Palm Beach Gardens, specifically in the Avenir community off Northlake Boulevard. The facility is expected to begin serving patients in early 2028 and will be designed to meet the healthcare needs of approximately 40,000 residents in the surrounding area. The 29-bed hospital will offer 24-hour emergency services and four operating rooms. JMC President and CEO Dr. Amit Rastogi described it as a neighborhood hospital aligned with the organization's commitment to serving underserved areas.

The new hospital directly responds to concerns raised by residents about healthcare access in western Palm Beach Gardens. Mayor Dana Middleton, who lives in the western portion of the city, pointed to construction that shut down Northlake Boulevard at the Beeline Highway last summer as a moment when residents' primary worry became clear. "Their No. 1 concern was, 'How am I going to get to the hospital? How am I going to get to my doctors?' And we're taking away that concern of traveling," Middleton said. Noel Martinez, president of the Palm Beach North Chamber, emphasized that healthcare access is a critical factor when businesses evaluate whether to relocate or expand in a region, alongside considerations about schools and transportation infrastructure.

The Jupiter Medical Center expansion represents part of a broader wave of medical facility growth in the area. Miller Medical Center opened in April in Palm Beach Gardens, making it the first full-service hospital to open in the region since 1979. Earlier in the year, Jupiter Medical Center also completed a new 92-bed Patient Care Tower, demonstrating the organization's significant investment in expanding healthcare infrastructure throughout the community.

Several healthcare providers expressed interest in partnering with developers on the new health complex, but Jupiter Medical Center ultimately secured the opportunity to establish the largest presence. Rastogi emphasized that the size and scope of the facility were carefully planned to ensure the hospital could provide appropriate services for the population it will serve. The decision reflects JMC's strategic positioning as a major healthcare provider in one of the region's fastest-growing areas.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves $1.3 million treatment plan for Sawgrass Lakes water issues
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie city council approved funding for a three-year treatment plan to address water quality problems in the Sawgrass Lakes community after a fish kill wiped out around 1,100 fish.
cards.body:
On Monday, Port St. Lucie city council approved approximately $1.3 million in funding for a three-year treatment plan to address water quality issues in the Sawgrass Lakes community stormwater tract using a solution called TryMarine. The city will continue working with their vendor, SOLitude, to conduct the treatment and test water quality. Kevin Matyjaszek, utility systems director for Port St. Lucie, said the city wants to ensure the chemistry is handled correctly.

The treatment plan comes after a fish kill several weeks ago that wiped out around 1,100 fish in the stormwater tract. Bob Shonce, HOA president of North Panther Trace at Sawgrass Lakes, said he and other neighbors have observed water quality changes for over five years. In March, city staff addressed community concerns, and most residents voted to move forward with TryMarine. Matyjaszek explained that the stormwater tract has muck and sediment issues that lower oxygen levels and water quality, making it susceptible to algae growth. However, Jim Moir, executive director of the Indian Riverkeeper, cautioned that while TryMarine may help reduce sediment, the city also needs to address where the muck originates, noting that an ongoing nutrient supply could cause the problem to recur.

cards.body:
The WPTV team spotted a giant truck at a recent Let's Hear It meet-up at the library in Belle Glade, where staff from West Technical Education Center were spreading the word about their programs. WPTV Morning Anchor Ashley Glass connected with the people behind the mission to train residents for employment. "West Tech is really appropriate for high school students and adults looking to learn a trade and get certifications that lead to work," Adrian Dowdell with the education center said.

West Tech offers programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and other fields. The center works with community and business partners to help people find work in Belle Glade and surrounding communities. For those unable to attend the monthly Let's Hear It meet-ups, WPTV invites residents to email LetsHearIt@wptv.com to share concerns and get answers to their questions.

cards.headline: Surfside condo collapse prompts Florida building safety reforms five years later
cards.teaser: Five years after the Champlain Towers South collapse killed 98 people, federal investigators concluded severe structural design deviations and construction problems caused the disaster.
cards.body:
The 12-story oceanside condominium known as Champlain Towers South crumbled to the ground in Surfside, Florida just after 1 a.m. on June 24, 2021, killing 98 people. In a technical report released Monday, federal investigators from the National Institute of Standards and Technology concluded the problem started three weeks before the collapse, when two connectors between garage columns and the pool deck failed, causing cracks to grow and loads to move to columns not strong enough to support them. Investigators traced the cause to severe and widespread deviations in the building's original structural design and standards of the day, and deviations in the building's construction from the design drawings.

The catastrophic failure exposed Florida's long history of lax building oversight. State lawmakers swiftly passed a series of new laws, including more stringent building regulations and mandates for structural inspections. Condominiums in the state are now required to maintain a minimum level of reserve funding for structural upkeep. The changes have prompted controversy, as higher HOA fees and assessments compelled many to leave condo living, forcing lawmakers to make additional adjustments to ease the financial burden. Federal investigators are now writing their final report and will include recommendations for changes to standards, codes and practices to improve building safety.

cards.headline: Breeze Airways adds five new routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport with fares starting at $79
cards.teaser: Travelers on the Treasure Coast will have five new flight options from Vero Beach Regional Airport starting this fall, with one-way fares starting at $79.
cards.body:
Breeze Airways announced five new routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport with one-way fares starting at $79. Travelers can book nonstop flights to Atlantic City and Trenton, New Jersey, and Baltimore, as well as one-stop, no-change-of-plane BreezeThru service to Burlington, Vermont, and Provo, Utah. Service to Atlantic City begins October 2 on Mondays and Fridays from $89 one way. Baltimore flights start October 1 on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays from $79 one way. Trenton service begins September 30 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, switching to Thursdays and Sundays beginning January 7, from $89 one way. Burlington service starts October 4 on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays, while Provo service begins October 2 on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays.

Breeze Airways, which started operations in 2021, currently operates more than 300 year-round and seasonal routes to 91 cities in the United States, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. The airport has increased flight options to serve the Treasure Coast's growing population. Passenger numbers at Vero Beach Regional Airport have seen dramatic growth in the last year. JetBlue began service to Boston and New York's JFK airports in December, and American Airlines began service to Charlotte in February.

Dr. Alyssa Comroe, CEO of Peggy Adams, told WPTV the safest place for pets during a hurricane is right alongside their owners. The shelter's expert team recommends several key steps for pet safety, starting with microchipping and ID. Pet owners should ensure pets wear a collar with current identification and have an updated microchip registered with correct contact information.

The organization also recommends introducing pets to a designated safe room ahead of time, such as a walk-in closet or downstairs bathroom, and conducting practice runs. Pet owners should prepare an emergency kit with a three-day supply of food and water in airtight containers, bowls, a sturdy carrier, bedding, towels, medications for two weeks, vaccination records, first-aid supplies, litter and box for cats, leashes, harnesses, cool packs, wipes, waste bags, and multiple forms of visible ID. Additionally, pet owners should keep a printed list of local pet-friendly shelters and hotels in an accessible place and maintain recent photos of pets, ideally with their owner, to help with identification if separated. Florida's hurricane season runs June through November.

cards.headline: Pioneer Park Aquatics Center in Belle Glade offers free swimming lessons for all ages
cards.teaser: Pioneer Park Aquatics Center in Belle Glade is offering free swimming lessons for infants as young as 6 months and adults to help prevent drowning deaths in the community.
cards.body:
Pioneer Park Aquatics Center in Belle Glade is offering free swimming lessons for infants as young as 6 months through adults. Stephanie Berry, the facility manager, said free swimming lessons are important to the community to avoid drowning deaths. "In the past 1-2 years, we have had a couple of drownings in our community. Swim lessons are so important, and we want to build water competency," Berry said. According to the Drowning Prevention Coalition of Palm Beach County, 41 children died from 2020-2024, with one of the most deadly areas being pools. Other dangerous water areas include canals, lakes, ponds, the Intracoastal Waterway and the ocean.

Reynaldo Perez Jr., a father of two, signed his kids up for the free lessons. "We live in Florida. I think everyone knows we are surrounded by water. Because of that, we want to make sure everyone has this skill in case we need it," Perez Jr. said. Berry noted that some parents never learned how to swim, so now they are learning alongside their kids. The program is being offered year-round. Registration is only available in person every other Saturday starting at 8:30 a.m., with lessons held Tuesdays through Fridays for two weeks.

hero.headline: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League urges South Florida pet owners to prepare hurricane disaster plans
hero.teaser: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create a disaster plan for their pets before the next storm hits. The safest place for pets during a hurricane is right alongside their owners, according to CEO Dr. Alyssa Comroe.
hero.body:
As hurricane season approaches, Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is calling on South Florida residents to develop comprehensive disaster plans for their pets before the next storm arrives. Dr. Alyssa Comroe, the organization's CEO, emphasized to WPTV that pets should remain with their owners throughout a hurricane rather than being left behind or separated during evacuation. The shelter's team of experts has identified several essential steps that pet owners should take now to protect their animals when severe weather strikes.

Proper identification is the foundation of pet safety during hurricanes. The rescue league recommends that all pets wear collars with current identification information and have updated microchips registered with accurate contact details. Additionally, pet owners should familiarize their animals with a designated safe room in advance, such as a walk-in closet or downstairs bathroom. Conducting practice runs before an actual hurricane ensures that pets will be comfortable entering this space when needed and reduces their stress during the actual emergency.

Preparing a dedicated pet emergency kit is equally important. This kit should contain a three-day supply of food and water stored in airtight containers, food and water bowls, a sturdy carrier for transport, bedding, towels, and two weeks' worth of any necessary medications. Pet owners should also include vaccination records, first-aid supplies, and for cat owners, litter and a litter box. The kit should have leashes, harnesses, cool packs, wipes, waste bags, and multiple forms of visible identification. Beyond physical supplies, pet owners should maintain a printed list of local pet-friendly shelters and hotels in an easily accessible location and keep recent photographs of their pets, ideally showing the animal with their owner, to aid in identification if pets become separated.

Storm preparedness should include practicing regular hurricane drills that incorporate pets' daily routines. Running through feeding schedules, water provision, and rest periods inside the safe room helps pets acclimate and maximizes their comfort during an actual emergency. With Florida's hurricane season running from June through November and overlapping with extreme summer heat, pet owners should also implement year-round heat safety measures including water enrichment, adequate shade, and limiting outdoor activity during the hottest parts of the day. Taking these proactive steps now can significantly reduce risks during evacuations and help ensure that pets remain safe and healthy throughout severe weather events.

cards.headline: Florida Mango Festival Saturday in West Palm Beach features 75 vendors, rare varieties and grower workshops
cards.teaser: Florida-grown mangoes will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beach County Convention Center.
cards.body:
Florida-grown mangoes will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beach County Convention Center. Organizers said the event will feature more than 75 vendors serving up local mango varieties, grafted trees, tropical fruits, and mango-themed products. Alex Salazar of Tropical Acres Farms told WPTV the indoor, air-conditioned venue offers an ideal setting for people to taste, learn, and discover the magic of Florida-grown mangoes without worrying about the summer heat.

Festival co-organizer Vince Rogers previewed some of the state's most unique varieties, including Fruit Cocktail, a sweet, multi-layered flavor; Orange Sherbet, offering creamy citrus notes; and Pineapple Pleasure, with tropical pineapple undertones. Rogers noted that Florida hosts more than 350 mango varieties, far beyond what's typically available in grocery stores. Throughout the day, visitors can attend educational talks on home mango growing and grafting techniques led by Salazar. Additional features include an "ID Your Mango" booth, a scion exchange for online mango community members, and a master display of Florida's diverse mango cultivars. The festival opens at 10:30 a.m. Saturday at 650 Okeechobee Blvd., with first pick ticket holders able to enter at 9 a.m. Garage parking is included with ticket purchase. Tickets and information are available at floridamangofestival.com.

cards.teaser: Meals on Wheels of the Palm Beaches has opened its new headquarters in West Palm Beach, upgrading from a cramped 1,200-square-foot office to a more than 4,000-square-foot facility. CEO Pamela Calzadilla called the move a gamechanger for the mission to serve homebound seniors.
cards.body:
Meals on Wheels of the Palm Beaches has opened a new headquarters in West Palm Beach, expanding from a 1,200-square-foot office to a more than 4,000-square-foot facility. The organization, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that receives no federal or local government funding, now houses administration, a commercial-grade kitchen, volunteer training space and collaboration areas under one roof. CEO Pamela Calzadilla said the expansion allows the organization to create more meals, store more fresh ingredients in a new walk-in fridge, and train volunteers on-site.

The $1 million gift from Sy and Nancy Taxman through the Taxman Family Foundation made the move possible. The new building is called the Meals on Wheels of the Palm Beaches, The Taxman Family Foundation Center. Volunteer Coordinator Kendra Grillo said housing staff and volunteers in the same location will improve operations and morale. Calzadilla stressed that homebound seniors in Palm Beach County rely on daily meal deliveries year-round, including during summer months when donations and volunteer numbers often decline.

hero.headline: Miami-Dade plans permanent conservation use for Alligator Alcatraz site after detention center closure
hero.body:
Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava announced plans to transfer all county-owned land at the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport to the National Park Service or other Everglades restoration partners once the Alligator Alcatraz immigration detention facility closes. In a Thursday memo to County Commissioners, Levine Cava stated her administration intends to pursue the transfer of the roughly 17,000-acre wetlands area within Big Cypress National Preserve for permanent conservation use as part of the Central Everglades Restoration Plan.

Levine Cava argued that the remote site has limited value as an aviation asset, pointing to high maintenance costs and flight restrictions due to its location near sensitive wetlands. She wrote that returning the lands to conservation represents "a historic opportunity to permanently protect these lands and contribute meaningfully to one of the most ambitious environmental restoration efforts in the nation." The transfer would also reduce county liabilities associated with managing an aviation facility with minimal strategic utility while creating opportunities to leverage federal restoration funding. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed that all detainees at the facility had been transferred to federal sites for their safety ahead of hurricane season.

The facility opened July 3, 2025, and has faced harsh criticism from lawyers, families and human rights groups over conditions and treatment of detainees. Detainees have reported poor physical conditions including worms in food, nonfunctioning toilets, flooding with fecal waste, and pervasive mosquitoes and insects. The detention center has cost far more than anticipated, with vendor contracts exceeding 824 million dollars for operations and maintenance alone, not including construction. According to an analysis by The Atlantic, the expenses were so high that it would have been cheaper to purchase each of the approximately 1,800 men detained there a one-bedroom condominium in Orlando and pay for a full-time personal guard. Florida has been approved for 608 million dollars in reimbursements but has received only 58.2 million dollars so far.

Levine Cava's administration will work with the County Attorney's Office and state and federal partners to identify legal transfer mechanisms, including conservation easements, deed restrictions, intergovernmental agreements, land exchanges or direct conveyance. Her office will provide formal recommendations to the Commission in the coming months. The transfer would permanently remove the lands from future detention, industrial or intensive commercial development and dedicate them to ecological restoration, habitat preservation and environmental protection.

cards.body: Gov. Ron DeSantis and White House Border Czar Tom Homan are holding a news conference Thursday morning at Alligator Alcatraz following reports that the detention center deep in the Everglades will close soon, nearly a year after its controversial opening that included a visit from President Donald Trump. State and federal officials have already moved detainees out, with ICE citing hurricane-season safety concerns. DeSantis has argued the temporary site served its purpose for immigration enforcement, but the closure follows months of criticism over the facility's cost, legal access, religious access and alleged treatment of detainees.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds committee launches $20 million statewide advertising campaign ahead of Republican primary
cards.teaser: Friends of Byron Donalds is launching a $20 million statewide advertising buy beginning Tuesday, June 30, and running through Primary Day on Aug. 18, the committee told Florida Politics exclusively.
cards.body:
Friends of Byron Donalds is launching a $20 million statewide advertising buy beginning Tuesday, June 30, and running through Primary Day on Aug. 18. The blitz spans cable, broadcast, streaming and radio across every major media market in the state, the largest single media investment the committee has made. The buy is built to blanket the airwaves with Donalds' pitch to protect the Florida dream by making the state safer, healthier and more affordable straight through the Republican Primary. Ryan Smith, Chair of Friends of Byron Donalds PAC, said the unmatched statewide media buy is the beginning of their strategy to tell Floridians how Byron Donalds is the only governor candidate of either party who will fight to lower the cost of living, hold government accountable for how it spends money, and protect the health and safety of families.

The Naples Republican, who represents Florida's 19th Congressional District, has spent the cycle leading the GOP field, with surveys showing him ahead of Lt. Jay Collins, investor James Fishback and former House Speaker Paul Renner by margins as wide as 40-plus points. One poll pegged his support among likely Primary voters at 54%. Donalds' political operation has surpassed $81 million raised from more than 35,000 donors and carried roughly $65 million in the bank into mid-June, a war chest that dwarfs the rest of the field and bankrolls a ground game the committee says has knocked more than 150,000 doors. Donalds became the clear front-runner after President Donald Trump backed him in February 2025, and has since added Donald Trump Jr., Elon Musk, the late Charlie Kirk, U.S. Senator Rick Scott, the majority of Florida's sheriffs and dozens of legislators and conservative leaders across the state.

cards.headline: Sen. Rick Scott explains how President Trump swayed Senate vote on Iran War Powers resolution
cards.teaser: Senate walked back a vote that would have urged President Donald Trump to remove troops from the Persian Gulf even as his administration attempts to negotiate an end to the conflict with Iran.
cards.body:
Sen. Rick Scott invited President Trump to a Senate policy lunch on Wednesday to discuss a measure that would have required troop withdrawal from the Persian Gulf. According to Scott on Fox and Friends, Trump told senators, "What the hell are you guys doing? I'm in the middle of a negotiation, trying to bring Iran to the table, and you guys say we have to withdraw troops. It's the craziest thing in the world. Why would you ever give the Iranians any idea that we're not united?"

Four senators initially voted for H. 86, a House-approved measure urging a defensive posture in the conflict: Bill Cassidy, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Rand Paul. Their votes made the Senate tally 50-46 in favor. Following Trump's lobbying, Cassidy flipped his vote and Paul voted present, while Collins and Murkowski maintained their original positions. Two additional Republicans who were absent during the initial vote subsequently voted against the resolution, shifting the final outcome to 47-50-1.

cards.headline: Lincoln Project launches Florida ad series contrasting Abraham Lincoln with President Trump
cards.teaser: The anti-Donald Trump Lincoln Project is using the Great American State Fair to show how the current President does not measure up to Abraham Lincoln.
cards.body:
The Lincoln Project is launching a series of ads at the Great American State Fair comparing Abraham Lincoln to President Trump. The first ad focuses on Lincoln's 1858 speech accepting the Republican Senate nomination from Illinois, arguing that a nation cannot be half one thing and half another and survive. The spot contends that Lincoln was unique in declaring slavery wrong, and a narrator draws a parallel to today's dichotomy between democracy and autocracy, and rule of law versus rule of one man. Lincoln Project Executive Director Tessa Gould contrasts Lincoln's reinvigoration of American liberty, destruction of slavery, and establishment of a moral course that persists today with Trump's alleged dismantling of America's true foundations for success.

The campaign includes several ads rolling out over coming weeks. "Better Angels," launching Friday, argues that Lincoln's inaugural speech was an inflection point offering reconciliation, contrasting it with Trump's peacetime dismantling compared to Lincoln's wartime building record. "Suckers and Losers" explores the difference between a president who wept for the fallen and one who called them suckers, launching July 2 as the series' emotional centerpiece. "Character" releases July 4 and ties Lincoln quotes to America's 250th anniversary. The project is also producing podcasts featuring political consultant emeritus James Carville and lawyer Jeffrey Toobin.

The stations are anchored in Gainesville. The Jaguars also agreed to a deal with the UF College of Journalism and Communications that will provide students access to cover sports at the NFL level. Chris Gargani, Jaguars Vice President of Sales and Marketing and UF graduate, said the organizations are uniquely positioned as the first NFL team and elite research institution to combine gameday broadcast coverage with hands-on career development for emerging talent.

UF students in the College of Journalism and Communications will work alongside WRUF staff and faculty to gain professional-level access. Student reporters and photojournalists will receive press box access, locker room availability and participation in press conferences before and after games at EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville this year. The radio deal spans three years. Hub Brown, Dean of UF's College of Journalism and Communications, said the college is committed to providing hands-on learning through this partnership. Beyond the fall game schedule, UF students will also be permitted to report on practices and training camp activities through the summer.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves $1.3 million water treatment plan for Sawgrass Lakes after fish kill
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city council approved funding Monday for a $1.3 million three-year treatment plan to address water quality problems in the Sawgrass Lakes community stormwater tract. The decision follows a fish kill that wiped out around 1,100 fish in the tract a few weeks ago. The city will use a solution called TryMarine applied by vendor SOLitude to treat the water and continue testing water quality.

Bob Shonce, HOA president of North Panther Trace at Sawgrass Lakes, said neighbors have been seeing changes in the water for over five years. Most of the community voted in March to try TryMarine after city staff listened to their concerns. Kevin Matyjaszek, utility systems director for Port St. Lucie, said the stormwater tract has muck and sediment issues that lower oxygen levels and water quality, making it susceptible to algae growth. Matyjaszek said TryMarine could help reduce the muck and bring oxygen levels back. Jim Moir, executive director of the Indian Riverkeeper, said while TryMarine may help reduce sediment, it may not solve the issue of where the muck originates. Moir said the city needs to do something proactive and immediate but also needs to look at the underlying issue, warning that if an ongoing nutrient supply continues, the problem will happen again.

cards.headline: Driver crashes into Hobe Sound water plant pipe, flees scene, leaving hundreds without water
cards.teaser: A driver crashed into a large pipe at the Hobe Sound/Osprey Water Plant and fled the scene Wednesday night, leaving hundreds of homes without water service or a.
cards.body:
A driver crashed into a large pipe at the Hobe Sound/Osprey Water Plant and fled the scene Wednesday night, leaving hundreds of homes without water service or adequate water pressure, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The crash occurred around 9 p.m. The driver was located after a family member brought him to the hospital for injuries sustained in the crash. Eliuvar Garza, 24, of Stuart has been charged with leaving the scene of a crash with property damage, driving with a suspended license with knowledge, failure to use due care, and failure to stop at a stop sign. A witness reported that Garza repeatedly stated "I messed up" before running from the scene.

Water services are now fully restored in the area, according to the South Martin Regional Utility. SMRU posted an advisory on its website stating that customers affected by the water shortage should boil their water for three minutes before using it. The SMRU emergency response team has restored water to all customers affected by this incident. The boil water warning remains in effect until further notice. Hobe Sound residents with questions about their water service should contact the water company directly.

cards.headline: Strong storms topple trees, damage property in Royal Palm Beach and Wellington
cards.teaser: Severe thunderstorms swept through Royal Palm Beach and Wellington Wednesday night, bringing down trees, damaging fences and knocking down light poles.
cards.body:
Strong thunderstorms swept through Royal Palm Beach and Wellington Wednesday night, toppling trees, twisting fences and knocking down light poles across both communities. A large tree was uprooted and fell into the road in one Royal Palm Beach neighborhood, blocking traffic. Firefighters responded and pulled the tree from the road so neighbors could clear it. Hail pelted cars, lightning struck close to residents and strong winds caused widespread damage throughout the area.

Seven-year-old Danny Jaworski was home with his grandmother when the storm hit. "I heard a cracking sound and then a boom," Danny said. Danny and his grandmother watched as the massive tree came down in front of a car driving down their street, blocking the road. Danny's mother, Leslie Jaworski, owns the home, which had been named the neighborhood's Home of the Month. She was at work when the storm hit and came home to find firefighters already on scene working to clear the tree. "I was grateful that the tree didn't go this way and land on my roof, because I've heard horror stories of that. I was grateful that the traffic was able to get through," Leslie said. The experience has her thinking ahead to future storms. "I'm a new homeowner, so it does kind of make me worried about future storms and what can happen," Leslie said.

cards.headline: Speeding Jeep triggers eight-vehicle pileup in Lantana, killing 67-year-old man
cards.teaser: A Jeep Wrangler speeding on Dixie Highway in Lantana struck a truck and caused an eight-vehicle pileup that killed one man and seriously injured others.
cards.body:
A speeding Jeep Wrangler triggered an eight-vehicle pileup on Dixie Highway in Lantana on Tuesday, killing 67-year-old Jose Bedoya and seriously injuring others. Sal Perna, who owns a car rental business near the scene, witnessed the Jeep traveling at extreme speeds before the crash. "I saw this Jeep, 4-door Jeep go by here at I would guesstimate 100 mph," said Perna. Investigators say the Jeep hit a truck near Ocean Avenue and Dixie Highway, fled the scene, then slammed into stopped traffic, causing the pileup. Two people were transported from the scene by helicopter. A GoFundMe has been set up to support Bedoya's family.

Bedoya's son shared a statement remembering his father as "the most hard working selfless person to ever exist" and "the last person in the world to deserve leaving this world in such way." Perna said the scale of destruction was unlike anything he had seen in his 11 years at the location. "I was in shock that there were so many vehicles involved to the point where they were unrecognizable," Perna said. He is now calling for increased police presence on Dixie Highway, citing dangerous driving as a daily occurrence. Investigators confirmed the case remains an ongoing, active investigation regarding potential charges against the driver.

cards.headline: West Technical Education Center offers trade certifications to Belle Glade residents
cards.teaser: West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade is offering trade programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and other fields to help residents get trained and certified for work.
cards.body:
West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade is spreading the word about its many programs to get people trained and ready to find work. The center recently brought a giant truck to a Let's Hear It meet-up at the library in Belle Glade to connect with potential students. 'West Tech is really appropriate for high school students and adults looking to learn a trade and get certifications that lead to work,' Adrian Dowdell with the education center said.

Dowdell explained they have programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and much more. The center also works with community and business partners to help people find work in Belle Glade and surrounding communities. The programs are designed to provide hands-on training and industry certifications that prepare students for immediate employment in their chosen field.
